The '''Aso clan''' (阿蘇) is a Japanese clan associated with [[Aso Shrine]]. They descend from [[Kamuyaimimi]].<ref name="takano-2006a">{{Cite book |last1=Takano |first1=Tomoaki |title=History and Festivals of the Aso Shrine |last2=Uchimura |first2=Hiroaki |publisher=Aso Shrine |year=2006 |location=Aso Shrine, Ichinomiya, Aso City.|qq=}}</ref> The clan were originally [[Kuni no miyatsuko]]<ref name="louisfrederic-2002a">{{Cite book |last=Louis-Frédéric |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p2QnPijAEmEC&dq=%22Aso+uji%22&pg=PA58 |title=Japan Encyclopedia |date=2002 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-01753-5 |pages=58 |language=en|qq=}}</ref><ref name="matsunaga-naomichi-2023a">Matsunaga Naomichi: ''[https://archive.today/20231025020641/https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=8839 Kuni no miyatsuko]'', Encyclopedia of Shinto, retrieved 25 October 2023</ref> but after the abolition of the role they took on a priestly role at [[Aso Shrine]].  They share this history with the [[Izumo clan]] of [[Izumo-taisha]], the [[Owari clan]] of [[:en:Atsuta Jingu|Atsuta Jingu]], the {{ill|Munakata clan|ja|宗像氏|1=Munakata clan|fr|Clan Munakata|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Munakata clan|13=User:Immanuelle/Munakata clan|qq=}} of [[Munakata Taisha]],<ref name="matsunaga-naomichi-2023a" /> and the [[Yamato no Kuni no Miyatsuko|Yamato clan]] of [[Ōyamato Shrine]].
The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century.<ref name="takano-2006a" /> 
== History ==
{{ill|Richard Ponsonby-Fane|en|Richard Ponsonby-Fane|qid=Q3246771|lt=Richard Ponsonby-Fane|1=Richard Ponsonby-Fane}} divides the history of the Aso clan into three stages<ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a">{{Cite book |last=Ponsonby-Fane |first=R. A. B. |title=Studies In Shinto & Shrines |date=2016-05-11 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98322-9 |edition=1st |language=English |chapter=Aso clan|qq=}}</ref>
=== Origins ===
The Aso clan originally descended from [[Kamuyaimimi]], a son of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|en|Emperor Jimmu|qid=Q200188|lt=Emperor Jimmu|1=Emperor Jimmu}} and [[Himetataraisuzu-hime]].<ref name="takano-2006a" />
It is speculated that many members may be buried in {{ill|Nakadori Kofun Group|ja|中通古墳群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakadori Kofun Group|qq=}}.<ref name="道の駅 阿蘇 2020 x983">{{cite web | title=Aso Kofun & Shouranzan | website=道の駅 阿蘇 | date=2020-06-24 | url=https://www.aso-denku.jp/english/2020/06/aso-kofun-shouranzan/ | language=ja | access-date=2023-10-25|qq=}}</ref>
Takashi Tanaka did research on their genealogy.<ref>Masanobu Suzuki: ''[https://www.waseda.jp/inst/wias/assets/uploads/2018/09/RB007-017-027.pdf Methodology for Analyzing the Genealogy of Ancient Japanese Clans]'', WIAS Research Bulletin no. 7, 2015</ref>
The position of Chief Priest of Aso Shrine is hereditary and is passed down from generation to generation with the oldest male in the family becoming the new head of the shrine. The Aso family has the second oldest recorded lineage in Japan after the Imperial family.<ref name="Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan y245">{{cite web | first=Zaynab |last=Nakhid |title=Friends of Japan Series: Japanese Shrines | website=Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan | url=https://www.tt.emb-japan.go.jp/itpr_ja/11_000001_00686.html | access-date=2023-10-25 |date=2019-10-09|qq=}}</ref><ref name="takano-2006a" /> The family themselves are said to be descendants of Takeiwatatsu-no-Mikoto.<ref name="takano-2006a" />

{{Tree chart/end|qq=}}In recorded history the family started as Imperial representatives called [[Kuni no miyatsuko]]. They looked after worship activities in their area. As they gained power, they became leaders in the Aso district. During this time they were very powerful.<ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a" />
=== Decline in the Nanboku-chō period ===
In the {{ill|Nanboku-chō period|en|Nanboku-chō period|qid=Q264012|lt=Nanboku-chō period|1=Nanboku-chō period}}, the Aso family faced problems.<ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a" /> They strongly supported the [[Southern Court]].<ref name="louisfrederic-2002a" /><ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a" /> This choice, along with family disagreements, weakened their power. Powerful military families like {{ill|Shimazu clan|en|Shimazu clan|qid=Q1061406|lt=Shimazu|1=Shimazu clan}} and {{ill|Ōmura clan|en|Ōmura clan|qid=Q385522|lt=Omura|1=Ōmura clan}} also became strong competitors. However, the Aso family always had a leader, known as the Daiguji. But many family members faced difficulties. Many died, others moved away, and some hid in the mountains.<ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a" />
=== Changes in the Tensho Period ===
During the Tensho period, {{ill|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|en|Toyotomi Hideyoshi|qid=Q187550|lt=Toyotomi Hideyoshi|1=Toyotomi Hideyoshi}} invaded Satsuma. The Aso family's leader, the Daiguji {{ill|Aso Koremitsu|en|Aso Koremitsu|qid=Q4807470|lt=Aso Koremitsu|1=Aso Koremitsu}}, was a young child then. They were slow in welcoming Hideyoshi<ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a" /> and were murdered in 1593 at the age of 12.<ref name="Institut für Japanologie an der Universität Wien 1975 p. 112">{{cite book | title=Beiträge zur Japanologie | publisher=Institut für Japanologie an der Universität Wien | issue=Bd. 12 | year=1975 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n8c4AQAAIAAJ | language=de | access-date=2023-10-25 | page=112|qq=}}</ref> But in the {{ill|Keichō|en|Keichō|qid=Q1328185|lt=Keicho era|1=Keichō}} (1596-1614), things improved for the Aso family. {{ill|Katō Kiyomasa|en|Katō Kiyomasa|qid=Q1069843|lt=Kato Kiyomasa|1=Katō Kiyomasa}} got control of the Higo province and helped the Aso family. He brought back old traditions and supported the old {{ill|Shake (social class)|en|Shake (social class)|qid=Q11588367|lt=Shake|1=Shake (social class)}} families. But the Daiguji did not become a territorial magnate again.<ref name="ponsonbyfane-2016a" />
The Aso family were priests but also rose to power as a powerful samurai clan in the 11th century. They remained in prominence until the 16th century as their feudal lord continued to rule over half of what is now known as {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|qid=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture|1=Kumamoto Prefecture}}. This contributed economically to the family and the shrine, allowing them to rebuild shrine buildings and hold festivals. It also made it possible for them to establish branches of the Aso shrine in other locations. Some of those shrines still remain in up to 500 locations to this day. Koreyuki Aso (''Aso Koreyuki in Japanese name order'') was the 91st Chief Priest of Aso Shrine with his son being the 92nd.<ref name="takano-2006a" />
